summary: RFC 2026 describes how the IESG reviews Proposed Standards and characterizes their maturity. This document updates RFC 2026 with a more current and accurate characterization of what a Proposed Standard is.

plainLanguage.summary: A first draft of a rule is called proposed. This explains honestly how well-tested those drafts really are today.

questions: how mature is a proposed standard rfc
what is the difference between proposed standard and internet standard
subtitle: Updates how the IETF describes a Proposed Standard: stable, well reviewed and ready to deploy.

tldr.problem: Section 4.1.1 of RFC 2026 no longer accurately describes Proposed Standards after two decades of more thorough IETF review.
tldr.mechanism: It replaces that section with a new characterization: a Proposed Standard is stable, has resolved known design choices, has had significant review and has enough community interest.
tldr.outcome: Proposed Standards are described as good enough to deploy, and known limitations must be clearly stated in the document.

today: RFC 7127 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2026 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why the Old Text Was Replaced
sections.content: In the two decades since RFC 2026, the IETF has evolved its review of Proposed Standards, so Section 4.1.1 of RFC 2026 no longer describes them accurately. RFC 7127 updates only that characterization. It does not change the procedures for maintaining Standards Track documents in RFC 2026 and RFC 6410, which should be read alongside it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old description was out of date, so this swaps in a new one and leaves all the other rules alone.

sections.title: How Review Really Works
sections.content:
Proposed Standard is the entry-level maturity on the standards track, and the IESG must take a specific action to put a specification there. It was once intended that documents would advance to Draft Standard and then Internet Standard, but the RFC says this progression is rare. Many Proposed Standards are deployed and used extensively as stable protocols, and most popular IETF protocols remain at that level.

Such documents have had open development and review, usually including cross-discipline reviews and a security review, often strengthened by implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Most rules never move up the ladder because they already work fine. They get checked by many people first.

sections.title: The New Characterization
sections.content:
A Proposed Standard is stable, has resolved known design choices, has received significant community review and appears to enjoy enough community interest to be considered valuable. Implementation or operational experience is usually not required, but is highly desirable. The IESG may require it for specifications that materially affect core Internet protocols or have significant operational impact.

It will have no known technical omissions, and implementations can be deployed. It may still be revised if problems are found. An Internet Standard (Section 3.2, copied from RFC 2026) needs significant implementation and successful operational experience, and a high degree of technical maturity.
sections.plainLanguage: A Proposed Standard is a rule that is steady, well checked and useful. Making it a full Internet Standard needs proof from real use.

sections.title: Known Limitations and Security
sections.content:
The IETF may occasionally publish a Proposed Standard that has areas of known limitations. In that case, the known issues will be clearly and prominently communicated in the document, for example in the abstract, the introduction or a separate section.

The document says it does not directly affect the security of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: If a rule has a weak spot, the document has to say so up front.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
Housley, R., Crocker, D., and E. Burger, "Reducing the Standards Track to Two Maturity Levels", BCP 9, RFC 6410, October 2011.
